summary: Rules-clean and readable from the two boundary rows, but the persistent design does not fix the problem it names. At T=753 with 264 programs, every program still walks ceil(753/264)=3 rows, so the tail is the same three row-times as the incumbent's waves. Chunked two-pass rows also keep fewer bytes in flight than a whole row in registers. Proceed, with a prepare-time sweep that also includes a single-wave one-row-per-program variant (num_warps 4, every row resident at once), with the parity gate relaxed to max 2 ulp plus rel L2, and on a81d19c.
justification: The floors and incumbent rows are those the held row-kernel's review verified: 12 B/elem x 8192 x T at 4.8 TB/s gives 15.4/61.7/335 us, against incumbent 20.5-23.0 / 74.7-79.6 / 396-400 us per boundary. The first_turn incumbent is already about 84% of the floor (about 4.0 TB/s, near practical HBM streaming), so the realistic gains are at turn_1 and turn_4: a few us per row and about 0.2-0.8% per shape, below headline drift. Judge on the rows (muse_spark_norm_residual_kernel x2 replaced by _boundary_persistent_kernel x2). The mechanism claim is 'no CTA launch waves (753 rows was ~3-6 waves)'. But the work unit is still one 96 KB row and the grid is 2 x SM = 264. Rows per program are 2 or 3, so the critical path is 3 row-times, the same quantization as 753 one-row CTAs at 2 per SM (2.85 waves). On H100, CTA launch costs well under 1 us per wave, so persistence removes almost nothing at T=753. What would fix the turn_1 tail is putting all 753 rows in flight at once: about 72 MB in about 15 us needs roughly 36+ KB in flight per SM, which a single wave of small one-row programs (num_warps 4, 6+ CTAs/SM) gives. Bytes in flight: chunking each row into 4 x 2048 columns with two passes means each program has about 12 KB (bf16 branch + fp32 stream chunk) outstanding, plus one prefetched chunk, about 24-48 KB per SM at 2 programs. The incumbent issues the whole 96 KB row at once. The persistent variant could therefore be slower at first_turn, where the incumbent is already near the floor. The alpha/beta/effective-weight vectors (fp32 [8192] x 3, 96 KB) cannot stay in registers across rows when rows are chunked, so the multi-row 'weights loaded once' advantage the earlier review pointed to does not happen; they are re-read from L2 every row, as in the incumbent. WEAKEST LINK: equal-sized row units mean a persistent grid cannot beat wave quantization at T=753. The win, if any, comes from the software prefetch overlapping one row's stores with the next row's loads, which is worth at most about one row-time out of three.
confounders: stack-tonight-five-prefill (landed, current master a81d19c): the spec says 'master (635cfee)', which is b92a0f4's submission blob. The stack does not touch either boundary (router GEMM, align, w2 zero-store, Marlin silu-mul), but it changes what runs just before ffn_boundary (expert output path) and so the L2 state of the branch input. Rebase on a81d19c and compare the rows against a81d19c's profile (c4d14d62f11e4aaf / 502f2eab95164781), not b92a0f4's.
sglang-pipeline-parity: it defines both boundaries as SGLang's FusedPostNormResidualPreNorm. The prepare() parity gate is against those same modules, which is the baseline, not a confound.

norm-residual-boundaries-triton-row-kernel (held, not run): the same math in a one-row-per-program structure. Since it never ran, this run's rows are compared directly with the JIT incumbent, and no stacking ambiguity arises.
interference: No companion run; the replaced rows are directly readable and nothing landed shares this launch or numerical path. The one-row-vs-persistent question belongs inside the run as a prepare-time sweep, not as a second check: {persistent 2 x SM, num_warps 8} vs {one row per program, num_warps 4, grid T} vs {one row per program, num_warps 8}. Time each with graph replays at T=753 and 3012 (and once at 16384), print '[boundary] variant ... us', pick per T band from shape only, and fall back to master's modules if nothing beats them by 2%. Prepare timings rank correctly even though they undercount (LESSONS 2026-10-25).
rules_flags: None blocking. alpha/beta and the effective weights come from SGLang's own precomputed modules in prepare() (parity, not a precision change). The stream stays fp32, the output bf16, and the internal math fp32.
NUM_SMS is read from device properties in prepare(), as a host int. Variant choice depends on T (shape) only, with no .item(), sync or timing in kernel_fn.

The parity gate 'bf16 max diff <= 1 ulp' risks a silent fallback: a different reduction order for sum(b^2) and sum(s_new^2) can flip roundings by 2 ulp on a few elements. Gate on max <= 2 ulp plus bf16 rel L2 <= 1e-5 and stream rel L2 <= 1e-6, and print the observed values (the earlier review raised the same point).
open_questions: At T=753, does a single-wave one-row-per-program variant (all rows in flight) beat both the persistent kernel and the JIT incumbent? That is the actual tail fix.
Does the chunked two-pass persistent kernel lose at first_turn, where the incumbent streams at about 4.0 TB/s? If it does, gate it to T <= 4096.

Does the JIT kernel round the normalized branch to bf16 before the residual combine? If so, the fp32-throughout math fails the stream rel L2 1e-6 gate. Check the sglang fused_norm_residual source before building.
